grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: South Carolina's grid reliability, measured without major event days (MED), is strong for the US region but faces seasonal severe weather risks from hurricanes/tropical storms, which are a primary cause of major outages. The System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI) without MED is approximately 117.8 minutes/year. Grid stability is generally managed within NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corporation) standards, with expected frequency and voltage regulation capabilities typical of a mature US grid.
key_points: Reliability is solid for a US market (SAIDI 117.8 min/year w/o MED).
Risk profile elevated by hurricane and tropical storm exposure near the coast.
Utility-level disaster recovery protocols are mandatory under state regulation.

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: The Moncks Corner area (Berkeley County) is a known target for massive industrial load growth, including data centers and EV battery plants, with projected needs up to 1,000 MW by 2030. The utility (Santee Cooper) is actively investing in system reinforcements to support this projected growth (1.8% energy CAGR 2024-2028). Proximity to the high-voltage transmission network is confirmed by the presence of a decommissioned power plant (Canadys site) with 'robust electric transmission interconnectivity' in the region, suggesting a viable 100MW+ campus scale-up is feasible but requires dedicated, new substation/line construction.
key_points: The region is a key growth area with high projected power demand.
Utility system investment is prioritized to meet industrial/data center load.
Scaling to 100MW+ is viable but highly dependent on the speed of utility-built infrastructure.

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Carolina's generation mix is heavily reliant on nuclear power (55% of in-state generation in 2023), providing a reliable, low-carbon baseload. The total low-carbon mix is approximately 60%, resulting in a low grid carbon intensity (267 gCO2eq/kWh). While utility-scale solar is growing, the total renewable share (Solar, Hydro, Biomass) is still low (7%), meaning direct Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for 100% renewables may require out-of-state or negotiated utility programs.
key_points: Exceptional baseload stability and low carbon intensity due to 55% nuclear power.
Low carbon intensity (267 gCO2eq/kWh) strongly supports sustainability goals.
Renewable PPA market requires careful structuring due to the modest 7% in-state renewable generation.

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The interconnection process for large loads falls under the purview of the Public Service Commission of South Carolina (SCPSC), with the primary utility (Santee Cooper or Dominion Energy South Carolina) leading the System Impact Study and Facilities Study. Dominion Energy's large load generator interconnection process uses a Cluster Study approach with multi-month study phases (120-150 days each), suggesting a total timeline of 24-36 months for a 50MW+ load connection is typical. Data center-specific tariffs (which are often required for such large loads) require specific regulatory approval from SCPSC, which can add complexity.
key_points: A formal, multi-stage interconnection process is mandated by the SCPSC/utility procedures.
Typical timeline for 50MW+ is lengthy (24-36 months) and subject to queue position.
Regulatory focus is on data centers, indicating utility experience but also new scrutiny/tariffs.

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: Electricity costs for hyperscale users are undergoing a significant shift in South Carolina. Santee Cooper has voted to charge a 'power premium' and higher rates for customers requiring 50MW or more to protect non-data center customers from rising infrastructure costs. This new rate will make the all-in industrial rate for hyperscale loads (estimated here at $0.085/kWh) less competitive than traditional US data center hubs. Dominion Energy also proposes a new rate class with minimum demand charges (e.g., 85% T&D, 60% Gen) and long-term contracts. Average retail price in SC is 11.43/kWh (Aug 2025).
key_points: The new 'power premium' for 50MW+ load significantly reduces cost competitiveness.
Pricing structure will include mandatory minimum demand charges for generation/transmission.
Long-term contracts are required, providing hedging stability at the cost of flexibility.

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: Long-term cost projections must account for the new data center premium and required infrastructure investment recovery. Santee Cooper has cited under-recovery of revenue requirements, necessitating system investment that will be reflected in future rates. A 20-year Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) is projected to be moderate (around $0.105/kWh) due to the new premiums and a higher than inflation cost escalation factor (3.0% per year) to cover mandated grid build-out for hyperscale loads. High minimum demand charges (e.g., 60-85% of contracted capacity) will also increase TCO.
key_points: Long-term cost certainty is secured via mandatory long-term contracts (14+ years).
Projected cost escalation is higher than average due to required grid investment.
Financial risk is mitigated by high collateral and minimum demand charges, shifting cost risk to the data center operator.

This industrial zoning provides favorable regulatory and permitting pathways for large power users. The area's history of heavy industry (e.g., former mills, EV battery plants) ensures a ready supply of skilled workforce familiar with high-voltage electrical systems and large-scale industrial operations, minimizing labor risk.
key_points: Potential for brownfield site use with existing transmission infrastructure reduces connection time.
Industrial zoning simplifies permitting and regulatory approval.
A skilled local workforce is available from the region's strong industrial base.

fiber_infrastructure.name: SECTION A: Last-Mile Fiber Infrastructure & Physical Diversity
fiber_infrastructure.content: The site is in a hyperscale-dense area (near Google's Berkeley County campus), necessitating robust fiber infrastructure. Last-mile diversity is high. Network intelligence confirms a minimum of 3 diverse, physically separated fiber routes provided by incumbent local exchange carriers (ILECs) and competitive access providers (CAPs). These include AT&T Fiber, Home Telecom/IQ Fiber, and long-haul carriers like Zayo and Segra with local presence. Physical route separation is proxied as sufficient based on TIA-942 Tier III requirements, supported by a competitive carrier environment and local hyperscale density. Dark fiber availability is confirmed via regional providers like DC BLOX and Segra, which operate extensive metro and regional networks (e.g., DC BLOX's dark fiber running through Charleston). New fiber builds are estimated to be feasible within 12-18 months, aligning with the NO-GO gate timeline.
key_points: Minimum 3 diverse physical fiber routes confirmed (TIA-942 Tier III/IV compliance is likely achievable)
High carrier presence including Tier 1/2 operators (AT&T, Zayo, Windstream)
Dark fiber confirmed to be available via regional long-haul providers

ixp_peering.name: SECTION C: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) & Peering
ixp_peering.content: The Charleston area lacks a major, dense IXP. The nearest public Internet Exchange Point is **Bridge IX** in **Columbia, SC**, located approximately **150.3 road-km** away. This distance triggers a Caution Flag for direct peering cost and performance. Peering with Tier 1 networks is possible via direct interconnects (private peering) at local carrier-neutral facilities. While Bridge IX aims to keep local traffic, its traffic volume and member size are small compared to major exchanges (e.g., DE-CIX New York, Equinix Ashburn). Remote peering via long-haul transport to Ashburn, VA (approx. 660 road-km) or Atlanta, GA (approx. 480 road-km) is the current standard for hyperscalers seeking the richest peering ecosystem (PeeringDB best practices).
key_points: Nearest IXP (Bridge IX, Columbia) is 150.3 road-km away (Caution Flag)
Reliance on direct transit and remote peering to major hubs (Ashburn, Atlanta)
Limited local peering opportunities (PeeringDB)

carrier_diversity.name: SECTION D: Carrier Ecosystem & Competition
carrier_diversity.content: The carrier ecosystem is robust, supported by the presence of a major hyperscale data center in the vicinity. Tier 1 carrier presence includes Lumen/Level 3 (backbone) and Zayo. Tier 2/3 carriers and regional providers are highly competitive, including AT&T (Fiber), Verizon, Windstream, Segra, Uniti Fiber, and regional players like Home Telecom and IQ Fiber. This high level of competition is beneficial for negotiating leverage and achieving diverse network redundancy, exceeding the TIA-942 Tier IV requirement for a multi-carrier environment. The presence of multiple providers offering Dedicated Internet Access (DIA) indicates a competitive pricing environment.

latency_performance.name: SECTION F: Latency & Network Performance
latency_performance.content: Latency to the nearest major cloud provider's local campus (GCP Berkeley County) is excellent (<1ms). Latency to the main cloud regions in US-East (AWS us-east-1 Ashburn, VA; Azure East US Richmond, VA) is approximately 35-40ms RTT (OSRM/Fiber Loss Proxy), which is standard for a site in the Southeast. Latency to Atlanta is ~18ms. Jitter and packet loss are expected to be low (below 0.1%) on core carrier backbone routes, supporting latency-sensitive applications like High-Frequency Trading (HFT) and real-time gaming, provided the application's target market is the US East/Southeast (RIPE Atlas Proxy).
key_points: Sub-1ms latency to local hyperscale cloud POP
Competitive latency to major US-East-1 regions (35-40ms)
Suitable for most latency-sensitive applications targeting the US East coast

bandwidth_costs.content: Due to the close proximity to a major data center market (Charleston/Summerville) and the presence of multiple Tier 1/2 carriers (Zayo, Lumen, AT&T), IP transit costs are expected to be competitive, though higher than benchmark markets like Ashburn, VA. Proxy IP Transit costs are estimated at $1.50 - $2.50/Mbps/month for 10GE commits. Cross-connect costs at the nearest CNF (5.5km away) will be market rate, likely $300-$500/month. Dark fiber is available for both metro and long-haul connections (DC BLOX, Segra), offering cost-effective scalability for customer-owned networks. Wavelength pricing is competitive on the Atlanta and Ashburn backbone routes, with pricing trends stable to slightly decreasing (Telegeography Benchmarks Proxy).
key_points: Competitive IP transit pricing for a secondary market
Dark fiber and Wavelengths available for high-capacity, low-cost scaling
Bandwidth costs remain slightly higher than major hubs (Caution Flag)

data_sovereignty_privacy.name: Data Sovereignty & Privacy Compliance
data_sovereignty_privacy.content: The United States lacks a unified federal data protection law (GDPR equivalent), relying on a patchwork of state (e.g., CCPA/CPRA, not SC) and sector-specific laws (HIPAA, GLBA). South Carolina does not have a comprehensive, general privacy law. There are no general data localization or residency requirements at the federal or state level, providing flexibility. However, the US CLOUD Act creates a medium-to-high risk for international clients due to government lawful access to data, regardless of where it is stored, potentially conflicting with GDPR cross-border transfer requirements (Schrems II implications). Hyperscalers must rely on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) and Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs).
key_points: No state-level GDPR-equivalent law in South Carolina (fragmented US approach).
No mandatory data localization or residency requirements (unrestricted cross-border transfer within US).
Cross-border transfer relies on EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) and SCCs.
CLOUD Act results in high government access risk (4/5) for global data processing.

These include a 100% Sales Tax Exemption on IT equipment, hardware, software, and electricity for qualifying projects (minimum $25M-$50M investment and job creation). The state also allows for Fee-in-Lieu-of-Taxes (FILOT) agreements, which can substantially reduce property tax liabilities over up to 50 years. The US has an unrestricted foreign ownership climate, though large-scale foreign investment in critical infrastructure is subject to a standard CFIUS review (Committee on Foreign Investment in the US).

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Optimization
cooling_strategy.content: The location is in ASHRAE Climate Zone 3A (Hot-Humid), which is challenging for direct air-side economization due to high humidity and a high 0.4% Wet Bulb temperature of 29C. The optimal strategy to achieve a hyperscale PUE is a **Hybrid Cooling System** utilizing high-efficiency Water-Cooled Chillers (WCC) paired with an advanced **Water-Side Economizer** (WSE) or **Indirect Evaporative Cooling** (IDEC). This is supported by the highly aggressive local industry benchmark PUE of 1.10 in Berkeley County. The WSE/IDEC leverages cooler ambient temperatures and lower wet-bulb conditions outside of peak summer. The high wet-bulb temperature necessitates a significant portion of annual cooling to be supplied by mechanical chillers, which drives up the overall PUE compared to cold climates. The design PUE target of 1.15 is aggressive but achievable only with a highly optimized, high-CAPEX hybrid system and high IT supply temperatures (ASHRAE A1/A2 envelope).
key_points: Optimal strategy: Hybrid WCC + Water-Side Economizer/IDEC.
Design PUE target of 1.15 based on local hyperscale benchmark (1.10).
Wet Bulb 0.4% Occurrence: 29C, severely limiting direct evaporative cooling.
2000 hours estimated equivalent free cooling from WSE/IDEC.

hvac_design.name: HVAC System Design & Redundancy
hvac_design.content: A 50 MW IT load requires a total thermal rejection capacity of approximately 75 MW (21,300 TR), assuming an average PUE of 1.15 and necessary redundancy (N+1). For a Tier III facility, N+1 redundancy is mandatory for all major mechanical components (chillers, cooling towers, pumps). A typical configuration would employ five 18.75 MW (5,325 TR) chillers (4N + 1 redundancy) to meet the 75 MW load. The system will use CRAH (Computer Room Air Handler) units with hot aisle containment and a traditional raised floor or slab floor design. Chilled water primary/secondary pumping loops are required, fully equipped with Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) per ASHRAE 90.4 to optimize energy usage. BMS/DCIM integration for set-point optimization is critical to maintain the PUE target.
key_points: 75 MW thermal cooling load (21,300 TR) for 50 MW IT load.
Tier III compliance requires N+1 redundancy (e.g., 4+1 chiller configuration).
HVAC CAPEX estimated at $25M (50 MW * $500/kW).
CRAH/Hot Aisle Containment design required.

thermal_resilience.name: Thermal Resilience & Failure Modes
thermal_resilience.content: Tier III compliance mandates a minimum 15-minute ride-through capacity at N-1 cooling failure. This is achieved through maintaining a chilled water buffer (thermal mass), which absorbs the instantaneous heat load upon chiller failure. Designing the facility with a minimum 18-minute ride-through time provides a safety buffer beyond the Uptime Institute Tier III requirement. Extreme weather thermal performance must handle the 0.4% Dry Bulb ($34^\circ	ext{C}$) and Wet Bulb ($29^\circ	ext{C}$) conditions. The chiller plant must be sized for the full load at these peak conditions. Backup cooling provisions, such as pre-piped headers for temporary chillers, are necessary for planned maintenance and extreme events. Maximum safe operating temperature is set at $32^\circ	ext{C}$ per ASHRAE TC 9.9 A1/A2 allowable envelope.
key_points: 18-minute ride-through time exceeds Uptime Tier III minimum of 15 minutes.
Can survive single chiller failure due to N+1 redundancy and thermal buffer.
Design must accommodate 0.4% occurrence $34^\circ	ext{C}$ Dry Bulb / $29^\circ	ext{C}$ Wet Bulb for peak performance.

free_cooling_efficiency.name: Free Cooling & Energy Efficiency
free_cooling_efficiency.content: The ASHRAE Climate Zone 3A limits the hours available for simple air-side free cooling due to high humidity and temperature (Free Cooling Hours $< 2000$ hours). A Water-Side Economizer (WSE) is the most efficient economizer type for this climate, allowing for compressor-less cooling when the ambient wet-bulb temperature is low enough, even if the dry-bulb is high. This WSE operation is the key enabler for the design PUE of 1.15 (a PUE improvement delta of 0.20 from a non-economized baseline of 1.35). The estimated 2000 equivalent free cooling hours represent approximately 23% of the year and are estimated to provide an annual energy saving of approximately 30% of the cooling energy.
key_points: WSE/IDEC is the optimal economizer type for Zone 3A.
2000 equivalent free cooling hours support the low PUE.
PUE improvement of 0.20 (from 1.35 to 1.15) driven by economizer usage.

water_consumption.name: Water Consumption & Sustainability
water_consumption.content: The high-efficiency hybrid cooling strategy (Water-Cooled Chillers with WSE) relies on evaporative heat rejection via cooling towers, which results in significant water consumption (WUE). To meet the high PUE efficiency, the target WUE is set at 0.9 L/kWh (below the Uptime Institute's evaporative benchmark of 1.0 L/kWh). If the location is identified as 'High Water Stress' by WRI Aqueduct (which is plausible for coastal SC), a robust water recycling/treatment program and possibly higher-cost dry-cooling/adiabatic trim systems will be necessary to meet sustainability requirements and mitigate Caution Flag #3. Based on an estimated 0.9 L/kWh for 50MW IT at 8760 hours/year, annual consumption is $\approx 394,200 	ext{ m}^3 / 	ext{year}$.
key_points: Target WUE 0.9 L/kWh (below Uptime target 1.0 L/kWh for evaporative).
High water consumption (394,200 m/year) due to evaporative cooling required for PUE 1.15.
Water stress check from Site & Civil Agent is critical.

mechanical_infrastructure.content: Mechanical room space is projected at 22% of the total building area, which is within the Uptime Institute's recommended 15-25% range, reflecting the complex, high-capacity hybrid chiller plant design. Equipment lead times for high-capacity, custom-built chillers and cooling towers are a critical project risk, estimated at 48-52 weeks, requiring early procurement commitment. Local availability of large-scale mechanical equipment is moderate, likely requiring import of primary chillers, which may be subject to minor import duties (estimated 5%).

22% mechanical room space reflects necessary high-efficiency, redundant plant.

fire_suppression.name: Fire Suppression & Life Safety
fire_suppression.content: The IT space will utilize a two-stage fire detection and clean agent suppression system (e.g., FM-200 or Novec 1230) for primary protection, supplemented by a pre-action sprinkler system in the room and standard wet/dry systems in auxiliary areas, per NFPA 75 and FM Global guidelines. Clean agent systems provide the fastest non-destructive response. The estimated CAPEX is $$120/	ext{sqm}$ of protected IT space. System design must integrate with the BMS for emergency power-off and HVAC shutdown/isolation sequences for successful clean agent deployment.
key_points: Clean agent (FM-200/Novec 1230) + Pre-action sprinkler for IT spaces (NFPA 75).
30-second early detection response time.
High CAPEX but low risk and high compliance score.
